title: A Borrowed Kinase, Straight to DNA

scenes.visual: Open on the carried world: a clean 16:9 cell cross-section filling the frame height—extracellular fluid at top, a horizontal plasma membrane across the upper third, open cytoplasm in the middle, and a gently curved nuclear envelope enclosing a soft violet (#A78BFA) DNA double helix at the bottom. Tiny ambient particles drift slowly so the frame is alive. Overlay bold title in crisp white: 'A Borrowed Kinase, Straight to DNA'.

scenes.tts: Add interferon to human cells, and genes switch on within minutes without new protein synthesis. How can a receptor with no enzyme reach DNA that fast? Every part of the relay must already sit inside the cell, waiting.
scenes.caption: Add interferon to human cells, and genes switch on within minutes without new protein synthesis. How can a receptor with no enzyme reach DNA that fast? Every part of the relay must already sit inside the cell, waiting.
scenes.visual: Title fades out. Warm amber (#F59E0B) interferon ovals drift down from top toward two slate-blue (#3B82F6) receptor rods crossing the plasma membrane. A subtle clock arc ticks at upper right labelled 'Minutes'. Inside the cytoplasm, dim translucent silhouettes of waiting proteins glow faintly while the violet DNA helix at bottom pulses with a glowing gene bar. Label the receptor 'No enzyme'.
scenes.narration: Add interferon to human cells, and genes switch on within minutes without new protein synthesis. How can a receptor with no enzyme reach DNA that fast? Every part of the relay must already sit inside the cell, waiting.

scenes.tts: Interferon is a cytokine, a small secreted protein carrying messages between cells. Each receptor chain crosses the membrane once and has no enzyme of its own. Instead, its inner tail holds a separate tyrosine kinase, called a Jak. That kinase waits there before any cytokine arrives.
scenes.caption: Interferon is a cytokine, a small secreted protein carrying messages between cells. Each receptor chain crosses the membrane once and has no enzyme of its own. Instead, its inner tail holds a separate tyrosine kinase, called a JAK. That kinase waits there before any cytokine arrives.
scenes.visual: Zoom smoothly onto the plasma membrane (subject filling >65% of frame height). Highlight the two separated slate-blue (#3B82F6) single-pass receptor chains, each extending a flexible intracellular tail. Attached near the membrane on each tail is a two-lobed JAK block: a coral-red (#EF4444) working kinase lobe and a muted rose (#FB7185) pseudokinase lobe gently breathing in idle motion. Labels: 'Cytokine', 'Receptor tail', 'JAK kinase'.
scenes.narration: Interferon is a cytokine, a small secreted protein carrying messages between cells. Each receptor chain crosses the membrane once and has no enzyme of its own. Instead, its inner tail holds a separate tyrosine kinase, called a JAK. That kinase waits there before any cytokine arrives.

scenes.tts: Each Jak has two lobes: a working kinase and a pseudokinase, an inactive look-alike that holds the real kinase back. When a cytokine binds outside, it brings two receptor chains side by side. Their Jaks now reach across, phosphorylate each other, and switch both kinases fully on. The receptor has borrowed an enzyme.
scenes.caption: Each JAK has two lobes: a working kinase and a pseudokinase, an inactive look-alike that holds the real kinase back. When a cytokine binds outside, it brings two receptor chains side by side. Their JAKs now reach across, phosphorylate each other, and switch both kinases fully on. The receptor has borrowed an enzyme.
scenes.visual: First show the muted rose (#FB7185) pseudokinase lobe pressing against the coral-red (#EF4444) kinase lobe, labelled 'Restrained'. An amber (#F59E0B) cytokine glides between the two outer receptor halves and draws the two slate-blue chains into alignment. As the chains settle side by side, the two JAKs rotate toward each other; bright gold (#FACC15) 'P' circles flash across from each kinase lobe onto the partner's activation loop, and both coral lobes brighten to active glow. Label: 'JAKs activate each other'. Empathy fix: Label the rose lobe 'Pseudokinase (inactive look-alike)' as it is named.
scenes.narration: Each JAK has two lobes: a working kinase and a pseudokinase, an inactive look-alike that holds the real kinase back. When a cytokine binds outside, it brings two receptor chains side by side. Their JAKs now reach across, phosphorylate each other, and switch both kinases fully on. The receptor has borrowed an enzyme.

scenes.tts: Next, the active Jaks add phosphate tags to tyrosines along the receptor tails. Those phosphotyrosines act as landing pads. A waiting protein called a Stat drifts up from the cytoplasm. Using its S H two domain, a pocket that grips phosphotyrosine, the Stat docks beside the active Jak.
scenes.caption: Next, the active JAKs add phosphate tags to tyrosines along the receptor tails. Those phosphotyrosines act as landing pads. A waiting protein called a STAT drifts up from the cytoplasm. Using its SH2 domain, a pocket that grips phosphotyrosine, the STAT docks beside the active JAK.
scenes.visual: Gold (#FACC15) 'P' tags pop onto tyrosine notches along the two slate-blue receptor tails. From the lower cytoplasm, two emerald-teal (#10B981) STAT blocks float upward; each STAT cartoon clearly shows a rounded notched pocket labelled 'SH2' and a short C-terminal tail carrying an unmarked tyrosine peg. One STAT glides up and clicks its notched SH2 pocket onto a gold 'P' on the left tail, and a second STAT docks on the right tail beside the glowing coral JAKs. Empathy fix: Show 'SH2 = grips pY' beside the docking pocket.
scenes.narration: Next, the active JAKs add phosphate tags to tyrosines along the receptor tails. Those phosphotyrosines act as landing pads. A waiting protein called a STAT drifts up from the cytoplasm. Using its SH2 domain, a pocket that grips phosphotyrosine, the STAT docks beside the active JAK.

scenes.tts: The Jak adds one phosphate to a single tyrosine near each Stat's tail. Notice what has changed. Each Stat already used its S H two domain to dock on the receptor. Now each carries its own phosphotyrosine, so what can two tagged Stats do next?
scenes.caption: The JAK adds one phosphate to a single tyrosine near each STAT's tail. Notice what has changed. Each STAT already used its SH2 domain to dock on the receptor. Now each carries its own phosphotyrosine, so what can two tagged STATs do next?
scenes.visual: Each glowing coral JAK transfers one bright gold (#FACC15) 'P' tag onto the tyrosine peg near the tail of its docked emerald-teal STAT. Briefly highlight both features on each STAT with crisp callouts: the 'SH2' pocket and the new gold 'P' tag. Both STATs gently bob as they loosen from the receptor tails, setting up the question.
scenes.narration: The JAK adds one phosphate to a single tyrosine near each STAT's tail. Notice what has changed. Each STAT already used its SH2 domain to dock on the receptor. Now each carries its own phosphotyrosine, so what can two tagged STATs do next?

scenes.visual: Hold the two phosphorylated emerald-teal (#10B981) STATs drifting gently just below the phosphorylated receptor tails, each clearly displaying its open 'SH2' pocket and glowing gold (#FACC15) 'P' tail peg. Display a clean high-contrast question card across the top: 'What can two tagged STATs do next?' Keep subtle ambient floating motion so the frame never looks dead, while giving 4.5 seconds of quiet thinking time.

scenes.tts: They trade one grip for two. Each Stat's S H two domain locks onto its partner's phosphotyrosine. Receptor docking is reversible. Once tagged, two reciprocal grips hold the active pair together, replacing one grip on the tail. The same S H two domain works twice.
scenes.caption: They trade one grip for two. Each STAT's SH2 domain locks onto its partner's phosphotyrosine. Receptor docking is reversible. Once tagged, two reciprocal grips hold the active pair together, replacing one grip on the tail. The same SH2 domain works twice.
scenes.visual: Question card fades. The two emerald-teal STATs detach from the receptor tails, rotate head-to-head, and snap together into a symmetric clamp: left STAT's SH2 pocket locks onto right STAT's gold 'P', and right STAT's SH2 pocket locks onto left STAT's gold 'P'. Briefly show a subtle comparison badge: '1 grip on tail -> 2 grips in pair'. Label: 'SH2 used twice'.
scenes.narration: They trade one grip for two. Each STAT's SH2 domain locks onto its partner's phosphotyrosine. Receptor docking is reversible. Once tagged, two reciprocal grips hold the active pair together, replacing one grip on the tail. The same SH2 domain works twice.

scenes.tts: Many Stats already rest in loose, inactive pairs. Phosphorylation flips them into this tight, active clamp. The active pair moves into the nucleus and clamps onto a specific DNA sequence to switch on genes. For some interferons, a third protein, I R F nine, joins the pair.
scenes.caption: Many STATs already rest in loose, inactive pairs. Phosphorylation flips them into this tight, active clamp. The active pair moves into the nucleus and clamps onto a specific DNA sequence to switch on genes. For some interferons, a third protein, IRF9, joins the pair.
scenes.visual: Pan smoothly downward following the locked emerald-teal STAT pair as it passes through a pore in the nuclear envelope and clamps snugly around the soft violet (#A78BFA) DNA double helix. A bright transcription arrow sweeps along the DNA. At lower right, a small labelled inset briefly shows a variant complex for type I interferon with a third soft-blue block ('IRF9') joining the STAT pair on DNA. Empathy fix: Open with a ghosted loose STAT pair snapping into the tight clamp; the IRF9 inset is labelled 'Some interferons: + IRF9'.
scenes.narration: Many STATs already rest in loose, inactive pairs. Phosphorylation flips them into this tight, active clamp. The active pair moves into the nucleus and clamps onto a specific DNA sequence to switch on genes. For some interferons, a third protein, IRF9, joins the pair.

scenes.tts: Step back and count the relay stages between receptor and gene. There is no second messenger and no chain of kinases. One borrowed kinase marks a waiting transcription factor that travels straight to DNA. Cytokine receptors borrow Jaks to send paired Stats straight to DNA.
scenes.caption: Step back and count the relay stages between receptor and gene. There is no second messenger and no chain of kinases. One borrowed kinase marks a waiting transcription factor that travels straight to DNA. Cytokine receptors borrow JAKs to send paired STATs straight to DNA.
scenes.visual: Pull back to show the full cell cross-section from membrane to DNA in one clean sweep. On the left, trace a glowing direct line from amber cytokine -> slate-blue receptor + coral JAK -> paired emerald-teal STAT clamped on violet DNA, labelled 'Direct relay'. On the right, show a faint dim schematic of a multi-step cascade crossed gently with a soft dash and labelled 'No cascade (schematic)'.
scenes.narration: Step back and count the relay stages between receptor and gene. There is no second messenger and no chain of kinases. One borrowed kinase marks a waiting transcription factor that travels straight to DNA. Cytokine receptors borrow JAKs to send paired STATs straight to DNA.

scenes.tts: This direct design serves most cytokine receptors. Both the borrowed kinase and the waiting Stat sit ready inside the cell. No new protein needs to be built first, so target genes can answer a surface signal within minutes.
scenes.caption: This direct design serves most cytokine receptors. Both the borrowed kinase and the waiting STAT sit ready inside the cell. No new protein needs to be built first, so target genes can answer a surface signal within minutes.
scenes.visual: Keep the full cell cross-section pulsing gently with one clean golden signal arc running from membrane receptor to active gene on DNA. Show two small tidy scope tags in the margin: 'Class I & II receptors' and 'Waiting parts -> rapid response'. Everything fades smoothly toward the end card. Empathy fix: Keep an on-screen tag 'Class I & II cytokine receptors'.
